title: Device inventory: Radiology prominence does not imply impact
desc: Documents specialty coverage and regulatory pathways without establishing clinical outcomes, workforce effects or distinct product counts.

kps.k: The FDA inventory documents a long history of AI-enabled medical devices, not evidence of their clinical or workforce impact.
kps.d: The Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Medical Devices list supplies regulatory records dated from June 1998 to March 2026. Its contribution to the debate is descriptive: AI-enabled products have a documented history in regulated medicine. The supplied material offers no comparative clinical results, adoption measures or workforce evidence, and advances no competing arguments. It therefore cannot establish that AI improves outcomes, replaces professionals or follows a particular adoption trajectory.

kps.k: The listed products span several medical specialties and tasks, with radiology prominently represented.
kps.d: The inventory includes image reconstruction, contouring, triage, ultrasound and planning products, alongside cardiovascular monitoring, neurological tools, ophthalmic devices, surgical systems and laboratory testing. This breadth documents varied applications rather than a single model of medical automation. Specialty classifications and product names do not establish clinical effectiveness or whether a device augments clinicians or operates autonomously.

kps.k: Different regulatory pathways require different descriptions of the listed records.
kps.d: The FDA inventory links K-number records to premarket notifications, DEN-number records to De Novo decisions and P-number records to premarket approvals, including supplements. Analysts should preserve these distinctions rather than describe every entry as an equivalent FDA approval. The links provide a route to investigate each device's regulatory record; the inventory alone does not supply a uniform assessment of performance.

kps.k: Versioned and repeated entries support product-history tracing, not straightforward counts of distinct technologies or evidence of improvement.
kps.d: The inventory records successive AutoContour versions from RADAC V2 in 2022 through V5 in 2026, and repeats some identical product names under different identifiers on the same date. Any analysis of technological growth should distinguish regulatory records, product families and versions. Repeated listings neither provide independent corroboration nor demonstrate better performance.

vlens.an: The supplied regulator source supports the cluster’s principal proposition, although it does so as a descriptive inventory rather than through an explicit argument. The FDA list documents AI-enabled medical-device records over a long period, with radiology prominent but products also classified under other specialties. Its identifiers and links also show materially different regulatory pathways, so the entries should not be treated as a uniform set of equivalent approvals. Nothing in the supplied material establishes comparative clinical outcomes, adoption levels, workforce effects, autonomy, or straightforward counts of distinct technologies. Because this professional-voice facet contains only one curated source, there is no basis for claiming broader regulator consensus or assessing cross-source prevalence. Internal variation lies in the inventory itself—across specialties, dates, pathways, and versioned or repeated records—not in competing regulatory positions.

elens.an: For the current-wave period, the supplied FDA inventory supports the proposition by functioning as descriptive regulatory evidence rather than evidence of impact. It documents AI-enabled medical-device records extending through March 2026, with radiology prominent but with entries also in cardiovascular and other specialties. It also contains different regulatory identifiers and successive product versions, reinforcing the proposition’s cautions against treating all records as equivalent approvals or as distinct technologies. Crucially, the inventory supplies no comparative clinical outcomes, adoption measures, workforce evidence or proof that later versions perform better. There is no material source-level disagreement because only one curated source is supplied; its internal variation concerns specialties, regulatory pathways and product versions, not competing positions on the proposition.
